concepts.name: Chemical equations
concepts.statement: A chemical equation represents a reaction symbolically: the formulas of the reactants on the left, the formulas of the products on the right, plus signs between formulas and an arrow between the two sides. Parenthetical abbreviations give the physical state of each substance (s, l, g, aq), and a word or symbol over the arrow, such as Δ for heating, names a special condition.

concepts.name: Coefficients give relative numbers
concepts.statement: The coefficients of a balanced equation state the relative numbers of reactant and product species, so they may be read as ratios in any amount unit: one molecule of methane and two of oxygen, one dozen and two dozen, or one mole and two moles. Note that the convention is to use the smallest whole-number coefficients, and that this reading is what makes an equation a statement about amounts rather than only about identities.

concepts.name: A balanced equation conserves atoms
concepts.statement: An equation is balanced when equal numbers of atoms of each element are represented on the reactant and product sides, which is what the law of conservation of matter requires. The number of atoms of an element is the coefficient of each formula containing it multiplied by the element's subscript in that formula, added over every formula on that side.

concepts.name: Balancing an equation by inspection
concepts.statement: Balancing by inspection changes coefficients, never subscripts, one element at a time until every element balances; changing a subscript would change the identity of a substance, as turning H2O into H2O2 turns water into hydrogen peroxide. A fractional coefficient may be used along the way and then cleared by multiplying through by a whole number.

concepts.name: Ionic equations
concepts.statement: A reaction between ionic compounds in water may be written with different levels of detail. A molecular equation writes every substance as a neutral formula; a complete ionic equation writes the dissolved ionic compounds as their dissociated ions; and a net ionic equation leaves out the spectator ions, which appear unchanged on both sides, so that it shows only the species that actually change.

concepts.name: Writing a net ionic equation
concepts.statement: Given a balanced molecular equation, the reader dissociates every dissolved ionic compound into its ions, identifies the spectator ions present in identical form on both sides, removes them, and reduces the coefficients to the smallest whole numbers. The result says, for example, that solid silver chloride forms from dissolved silver and chloride ions whatever their source.

concepts.name: Reactant
concepts.statement: A reactant is a substance undergoing a chemical or physical change, shown on the left side of the arrow in a chemical equation.

concepts.name: Product
concepts.statement: A product is a substance formed by a chemical or physical change, shown on the right side of the arrow in a chemical equation.

concepts.name: Coefficient
concepts.statement: A coefficient is a number placed in front of a symbol or formula in a chemical equation to indicate its relative amount.

concepts.name: Molecular equation
concepts.statement: A molecular equation is a chemical equation in which all reactants and products are represented as neutral substances.

concepts.name: Complete ionic equation
concepts.statement: A complete ionic equation is a chemical equation in which all dissolved ionic reactants and products, including spectator ions, are explicitly represented by formulas for their dissociated ions.

concepts.name: Net ionic equation
concepts.statement: A net ionic equation is a chemical equation in which only those dissolved ionic reactants and products that undergo a chemical or physical change are represented, so spectator ions are excluded.

concepts.name: Spectator ion
concepts.statement: A spectator ion is an ion that does not undergo a chemical or physical change during a reaction, but its presence is required to maintain charge neutrality.

concepts.name: Precipitation reactions and solubility
concepts.statement: A precipitation reaction is one in which dissolved substances react to form one or more solid products, often by an exchange of ions between ionic compounds. A substance precipitates when its concentration exceeds its solubility, the maximum concentration that can be achieved under specified conditions, so the insoluble compounds are the ones that come out of solution.

concepts.name: Predicting a precipitate from solubility guidelines
concepts.statement: To predict whether mixing two solutions gives a precipitate, identify every ion present, consider each new cation and anion pairing, and look each up in the solubility guidelines. If one pairing is insoluble, a precipitation reaction is expected and its net ionic equation can be written.

concepts.name: Acids and bases
concepts.statement: An acid-base reaction is one in which a hydrogen ion is transferred from one species to another. In water, an acid is a substance that yields hydronium ions, as hydrogen chloride does by transferring H+ to water molecules, and a base is one that yields hydroxide ions, either by dissociating, as ionic hydroxides do, or by reacting with water, as ammonia does.

concepts.name: Strong and weak acids and bases
concepts.statement: A strong acid reacts completely with water, so virtually every dissolved molecule yields a hydronium ion, and a strong base, such as an ionic hydroxide, dissociates completely. A weak acid or weak base reacts only partially, leaving most of its molecules in their original form, which is why its equation is written with a double arrow; only about 1% of acetic acid or of ammonia is ionized under typical conditions.

concepts.name: Neutralization reactions
concepts.statement: A neutralization reaction is an acid-base reaction whose reactants are an acid and a base (but not water), and whose products are often a salt and water. The net ionic equation for the neutralization of any strong acid by an ionic hydroxide is the same, hydronium ion and hydroxide ion giving water.

concepts.name: Assigning oxidation numbers
concepts.statement: The oxidation number of an element in a compound is the charge its atoms would have if the compound were ionic. It is assigned by four guidelines: zero in an elemental substance, the ion's charge for a monatomic ion, the usual values for hydrogen, oxygen and the halogens, and a sum equal to the charge of the molecule or ion, which fixes the one unknown. Note that an oxidation number is written sign first (+2), a charge number first (2+).

concepts.name: Oxidation-reduction reactions
concepts.statement: An oxidation-reduction (redox) reaction is one in which one or more elements undergo a change in oxidation number. Oxidation is an increase in oxidation number, or a loss of electrons, and reduction a decrease, or a gain; the reducing agent is the species oxidized and the oxidizing agent the species reduced. Defined this way, the class includes reactions such as hydrogen with chlorine in which no electrons are transferred outright.

concepts.name: Classifying a reaction
concepts.statement: Given an equation or a description, the reader should be able to say whether it is a precipitation, an acid-base or a redox reaction, or more than one, and name a redox subclass where one fits: combustion, in which a fuel and an oxidant react vigorously to give heat and often light, single displacement, in which an ion in solution is replaced through the oxidation of a metal, or disproportionation, in which one element is both oxidized and reduced.

concepts.name: Balancing redox equations by half-reactions
concepts.statement: A redox equation in aqueous solution can be hard to balance by inspection because water, hydronium ions and hydroxide ions take part. The half-reaction method writes the oxidation and the reduction separately, balances each for atoms (oxygen with water, hydrogen with H+) and then for charge with electrons, scales them to equal numbers of electrons and adds them, with extra steps that convert H+ to water in basic solution. Both atoms and charge must balance at the end.

concepts.name: Solubility
concepts.statement: The solubility of a substance is the extent to which it dissolves in water or any other solvent. A substance of relatively high solubility is soluble, and one that dissolves only to a slight extent is insoluble.

concepts.name: Salt
concepts.statement: A salt is an ionic compound that can be formed by the reaction of an acid with a base, containing a cation and an anion other than hydroxide or oxide.

concepts.name: Combustion reaction
concepts.statement: A combustion reaction is a vigorous redox reaction producing significant amounts of energy in the form of heat and, sometimes, light.

concepts.name: Single-displacement reaction
concepts.statement: A single-displacement (replacement) reaction is a redox reaction in which an elemental substance is oxidized by an ionic species.

concepts.name: Half-reaction
concepts.statement: A half-reaction is an equation that shows either the oxidation or the reduction of a redox reaction alone, with the electrons each reactant loses or gains.

concepts.name: Soluble
concepts.statement: A soluble substance is one of relatively high solubility, dissolving to a relatively large extent.

concepts.name: Insoluble
concepts.statement: An insoluble substance is one of relatively low solubility, dissolving only to a slight extent.

concepts.name: Precipitate
concepts.statement: A precipitate is an insoluble product that forms from the reaction of soluble reactants.

concepts.name: Acid
concepts.statement: An acid is a substance that produces H₃O⁺ when dissolved in water.

concepts.name: Base
concepts.statement: A base is a substance that produces OH⁻ when dissolved in water.

concepts.name: Acid-base reaction
concepts.statement: An acid-base reaction is a reaction involving the transfer of a hydrogen ion between reactant species.

concepts.name: Strong acid
concepts.statement: A strong acid is an acid that reacts completely when dissolved in water to yield hydronium ions.

concepts.name: Weak acid
concepts.statement: A weak acid is an acid that reacts only to a slight extent when dissolved in water to yield hydronium ions.

concepts.name: Strong base
concepts.statement: A strong base is a base that reacts completely when dissolved in water to yield hydroxide ions.

concepts.name: Weak base
concepts.statement: A weak base is a base that reacts only to a slight extent when dissolved in water to yield hydroxide ions.

concepts.name: Oxidation number
concepts.statement: The oxidation number, or oxidation state, of an element in a compound is the charge each of its atoms would have if the compound were ionic.

concepts.name: Oxidation
concepts.statement: Oxidation is the process in which an element’s oxidation number is increased by loss of electrons.

concepts.name: Reduction
concepts.statement: Reduction is the process in which an element’s oxidation number is decreased by gain of electrons.

concepts.name: Oxidizing agent
concepts.statement: An oxidizing agent, or oxidant, is a substance that brings about the oxidation of another substance and in the process becomes reduced.

concepts.name: Reducing agent
concepts.statement: A reducing agent, or reductant, is a substance that brings about the reduction of another substance and in the process becomes oxidized.

concepts.name: Reaction stoichiometry
concepts.statement: The stoichiometry of a reaction is the set of quantitative relationships between the amounts of the substances it consumes and produces, and the balanced equation states it. As a recipe for eight pancakes scales to twenty-four, the coefficients scale to any amount of any reactant or product.

concepts.name: Stoichiometric factors
concepts.statement: A stoichiometric factor is a ratio of two coefficients from a balanced equation, such as 2 mol NH3 per 3 mol H2 in the synthesis of ammonia, and it may be written in any amount unit. It is the one step every reaction stoichiometry calculation shares, whatever quantities are given at its start and asked for at its end.

concepts.name: Mole stoichiometry
concepts.statement: Multiplying a given molar amount of one substance by the stoichiometric factor gives the molar amount of another, and Avogadro's number turns that molar amount into a number of molecules. This is the shortest stoichiometry calculation and the pattern the longer ones extend.

concepts.name: Mass stoichiometry
concepts.statement: Since masses, not numbers of molecules, are what can be measured, a practical stoichiometry calculation converts a given mass (or a volume of a solution of known molarity) to moles, applies the stoichiometric factor, and converts the result back to a mass or a volume. The route is the same whether the two substances are a reactant and a product or two reactants.

concepts.name: Limiting and excess reactants
concepts.statement: When reactants are not present in stoichiometric amounts, one is used up first and limits the amount of product; the others are in excess and some of each is left over. Eleven slices of cheese and twenty-eight slices of bread make eleven sandwiches with six slices of bread to spare, and three moles of hydrogen with two of chlorine make four moles of hydrogen chloride with one mole of hydrogen to spare.

concepts.name: Identifying the limiting reactant
concepts.statement: There are two ways. Compare the molar ratio of the reactants provided with the stoichiometric ratio of the equation, or compute the amount of product each reactant alone would give; the reactant that gives the lesser amount is the limiting one.

concepts.name: Theoretical and actual yield
concepts.statement: The theoretical yield is the amount of product the stoichiometry of the balanced equation predicts from the limiting reactant; the actual yield is the amount obtained, and it is often less because of side reactions, incomplete reactions and losses in collecting the product.

concepts.name: Percent yield
concepts.statement: Percent yield is the actual yield divided by the theoretical yield, times 100%, and it measures how efficiently a reaction delivered the product the stoichiometry allows. Both yields may be masses, molar amounts or any other measure, so long as they are in the same units, which then cancel.

concepts.name: Atom economy
concepts.statement: The atom economy of a process is the mass of the desired product as a percentage of the mass of all the reactants used, a measure of how much of what goes in ends up in the product. It looks like percent yield but compares the theoretical efficiencies of different processes, whereas percent yield compares what one process actually gives with what it could give.

forms.condition: the theoretical efficiency of a synthesis, the mass of the desired product as a percentage of the mass of all the reactants used

concepts.name: Theoretical yield
concepts.statement: The theoretical yield is the amount of product that may be produced from a given amount of reactant according to the reaction stoichiometry.

concepts.name: Actual yield
concepts.statement: The actual yield is the amount of product formed in a reaction.

concepts.name: Excess reactant
concepts.statement: An excess reactant is a reactant present in an amount greater than required by the reaction stoichiometry.

concepts.name: Quantitative chemical analysis
concepts.statement: Quantitative analysis is the determination of the amount or concentration of a substance in a sample, and reaction stoichiometry is one of its foundations: the amount of a reactant that combines with the analyte, or of a product it gives, measures how much analyte there was.

concepts.name: Titration analysis
concepts.statement: In a titration, a titrant of known concentration is added from a buret to a sample of the analyte until the reaction between them is complete. The volume of titrant needed to reach this equivalence point, detected as an end point by a change such as an indicator's color, measures the amount of analyte through the reaction's stoichiometry.

concepts.name: Calculating a concentration from titration data
concepts.statement: The volume and molarity of the titrant give its molar amount, the stoichiometric factor gives the molar amount of analyte, and dividing by the sample volume gives the analyte's molarity. Since molarity is also millimoles per milliliter, the calculation can be done in milliliters throughout.

concepts.name: Gravimetric analysis
concepts.statement: In a gravimetric analysis the analyte is separated from the sample by a change of state, often by precipitation and filtration, and weighed; the mass of the isolated substance, carried through the stoichiometry, gives the mass of the analyte and its percent of the sample.

concepts.name: Combustion analysis
concepts.statement: A weighed sample of a compound of carbon and hydrogen is burned completely in oxygen, and the carbon dioxide and water it gives are collected in separate preweighed absorbers. The mass of each product gives the moles of carbon and of hydrogen in the sample, and their smallest whole-number ratio gives the empirical formula.

concepts.name: Analyte
concepts.statement: An analyte is the chemical species of interest in an analysis.

concepts.name: Titrant
concepts.statement: A titrant is a solution containing a known concentration of a substance that will react with the analyte in a titration analysis.

concepts.name: Buret
concepts.statement: A buret is a device used for the precise delivery of variable liquid volumes, as in a titration analysis.

concepts.name: Equivalence point
concepts.statement: The equivalence point is the volume of titrant solution required to react completely with the analyte in a titration analysis, a stoichiometric amount of titrant for the sample’s analyte.

concepts.name: End point
concepts.statement: The end point is the measured volume of titrant solution that yields the change in the sample’s appearance or other property expected for stoichiometric equivalence.

concepts.name: Indicator
concepts.statement: An indicator is a substance added to the sample in a titration analysis to permit visual detection of the end point.
